question: To whom does the author write, what does he sum up from the “first book,” and what happens on the mountain before Jesus is taken up to heaven?
The word μάρτυς (martys, “witness”) appears in the promise and in the choice of Judas's replacement: what is required of someone who is to be a witness?
The disciples ask about the restoration of the kingdom to Israel: how does Jesus' answer redirect their expectation and sketch the plan of the book?
Before any action, the group “continued with one accord in prayer”: how do you usually wait when you do not yet know the next step?
What signs accompany the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, where do those who hear come from, and how do different people in the crowd react?
The verb ἐκχέω (ekcheo, “pour out”) links Joel's prophecy to what the crowd is seeing: what image does this verb suggest about the way the Spirit is given?
How does Peter use David's Psalms to speak of Jesus' resurrection, and to what conclusion does he lead “all the house of Israel”?
In answer to the question “what shall we do?”, what does Peter propose, and how do the Christian traditions usually relate repentance, baptism and the gift of the Spirit?
Of the practices of the first community (teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers, sharing), which is most absent from your life of faith today?
Where and at what hour does the encounter with the lame man take place, what does he expect to receive, and what does Peter give him?
To whom does Peter attribute the healing, and why does he insist on setting aside the idea of “our own power or godliness”?
The verb μετανοέω (metanoeo, “repent, change one's mind”) appears right after Peter speaks of the people's ignorance: what does this call propose to the hearers?
“Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you”: what do you have to offer someone, even without material resources?
Who arrests Peter and John, for what reason, and what question does the council ask them the next day?
The word παρρησία (parresia, “boldness, freedom to speak”) marks the beginning and the end of the chapter: where does this boldness come from, according to the text itself?
How do Peter and John justify disobeying the council's order, and what criteria does the text offer for thinking about the relationship between human authority and God?
How is the sharing of goods described here, and what role does Barnabas's example have in the transition to the next chapter?
Threatened, the community does not ask for protection but for boldness: what would you ask of God in a similar situation of pressure?
What do Ananias and Sapphira do with the price of the property, and what does Peter say was in their power before and after the sale?
Why does this harsh episode appear right after Barnabas's generous example, and how should we read such a severe account of judgment today?
The verb πειθαρχέω (peitharcheo, “obey”) appears in the apostles' answer to the council: to whom do they say they owe obedience, and with what argument?
What reasoning does Gamaliel present to the council, and what value and what limits does the criterion “if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them” have?
The apostles leave flogged and “rejoicing”: what can make someone able to suffer for a conviction without bitterness?
What complaint arises in the community, who makes it, and what solution do the Twelve propose and the community accept?
The word διακονία (diakonia, “service, ministry”) is used both for the distribution of food and for the word: what does this suggest about the value of each task?
What accusations are raised against Stephen, and why are the temple and the Law such sensitive subjects for his accusers?
The complaint of the Grecian widows reveals people forgotten in the sharing: who may be left out in the community you belong to?
What phases of Israel's history does Stephen go through in his speech, and in what lands does God appear or act in each one?
What pattern does Stephen highlight in the way Joseph and Moses were treated by their own brothers, and where does he want to go with this?
The word σκηνή (skene, “tent, tabernacle”) appears when Stephen speaks of the place of God's presence: what does he want to show by saying that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands?
Stephen dies praying “do not hold this sin against them”: what does this prayer show you about forgiving those who hurt you?
What does the persecution after Stephen's death cause in the church of Jerusalem, and what happens in Samaria with Philip's arrival?
Why does Peter react so harshly to Simon's offer, and how do the Christian traditions usually understand the coming of the Spirit only after the apostles' arrival?
The verb εὐαγγελίζω (euangelizo, “proclaim the good news”) appears at several points in the chapter: who proclaims, to whom and in what places?
The eunuch asks “how can I, unless someone guides me?”: who helped you understand Scripture, and whom could you help?
With what intention does Saul go to Damascus, what happens on the way, and in what state does he arrive in the city?
The verb διώκω (dioko, “persecute”) appears in the voice's question: what does it mean for Jesus to say it is He whom Saul persecutes, if Saul was persecuting the disciples?
What objection does Ananias present to the Lord, what answer does he receive, and what is the weight of the first word he says to Saul: “brother”?
Why are the disciples in Jerusalem afraid of Saul, and what role does Barnabas play in his being accepted?
Tabitha is remembered for the tunics and garments she made for the widows: for what concrete care would you like to be remembered?
How is Cornelius described, where does he live, and what does the angel tell him to do?
What does Peter see on the roof, why does he refuse the command three times, and how does he himself come to understand the vision in verse 28?
The word προσωπολήπτης (prosopoleptes, “one who shows favoritism”) is used by Peter in the negative: what does he recognize about God before the household of Cornelius?
Peter says he learned not to call anyone “impure or unclean”: what kind of person do you tend to keep at a distance, and why?
What criticism do the circumcised believers make of Peter, how does he answer, and what conclusion does the group draw at the end?
What is new in the proclamation made in Antioch, and how does Barnabas react on arriving there?
The name Χριστιανός (Christianos, “Christian”) appears for the first time in Antioch: what kind of community receives this name, judging by what the chapter tells?
On learning of the famine, each disciple sends relief “according to his ability”: how can you respond, as far as you are able, to a distant need?
What does Herod do against the church, how is Peter guarded in prison, and how does he get out of it?
Why does the text dwell on the comic scene of Rhoda and those who were praying and did not believe Peter was at the door?
The word ἄγγελος (angelos, “angel, messenger”) appears in Peter's deliverance and in Herod's death: what contrast does the chapter draw between these two outcomes?
While Peter was in prison, “the church was fervently praying to God for him”: for whom could you pray with this insistence now?
Who was part of the church's leadership in Antioch, at what moment does the Spirit speak, and how are Barnabas and Saul sent out?
What moments of Israel's history does Paul choose to arrive at Jesus in the synagogue of Pisidian Antioch, and why does he begin with them?
The verb δικαιόω (dikaioo, “justify”) appears in contrast with the law of Moses: what does Paul affirm in these verses, and how do the Christian traditions usually explain this word?
What leads Paul and Barnabas to say “we now turn to the Gentiles,” and how do they ground this decision in Scripture?
John Mark leaves the team in the middle of the journey: how do you deal with someone who abandons a shared project, or with the time you were the one who gave up?
How does the crowd in Lystra interpret the healing of the lame man, and what do Barnabas and Paul do to stop the sacrifice?
Speaking to people who did not know the Scriptures, from where does Paul start in speaking of God, and what changes compared with the speeches in the synagogues?
The word θλῖψις (thlipsis, “hardship, pressure”) appears in the advice given to the new churches: why do the apostles speak of hardships right after being stoned?
Paul is taken for dead and, the next day, continues his journey: what helps you get up after a hard blow?
What teaching provokes the crisis in Antioch, who is sent to Jerusalem, and who gathers to deal with the question?
Peter calls the requirement a ζυγός (zygos, “yoke”): what does he set against this yoke in verse 11?
How does James bring together Peter's account, the prophecy of Amos and the final instructions to the Gentiles, and why these four abstentions in particular?
What disagreement separates Paul and Barnabas over John Mark, and what does the text leave open about who was right?
“It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us”: how do you seek to decide as a community when there are strong opinions on both sides?
What paths are closed to the team before reaching Macedonia, and how does the direction finally become clear?
Lydia, the slave girl and the jailer are very different people: what does the way each one encounters the Gospel show about the community born in Philippi?
The verb σῴζω (sozo, “save”) appears in the jailer's question and in the answer of Paul and Silas: what might the jailer have understood by “be saved” at that moment?
Imprisoned and wounded, Paul and Silas pray and sing at midnight: how do you react when you are “imprisoned” in a situation you did not choose?
What does Paul do for three Sabbaths in Thessalonica, what reaction does he provoke, and of what are Jason and the brothers accused?
Why are the Bereans called “more noble-minded,” and what does the way they receive the word teach about listening to preaching?
The verb διαλέγομαι (dialegomai, “reason, discuss”) describes Paul's method in the synagogue and in the marketplace: what does this verb suggest about the way he presented the faith?
At the Areopagus, Paul starts from the altar “TO AN UNKNOWN GOD” and quotes Greek poets: what bridges does he build with his hearers, and at what point does he part ways with them?
Some mock, others put it off and some believe: with which of these reactions do you most identify when faced with something that challenges what you think?
With whom does Paul stay in Corinth, how does he make a living there, and what does the Lord tell him in the night vision?
The text says that Paul and the couple were σκηνοποιός (skenopoios, “tentmakers”) by trade: what importance might the fact that the apostle worked with his own hands have?
How does Gallio decide the accusation against Paul, and what place does this decision by a Roman authority have in the narrative of Acts?
Priscilla and Aquila take Apollos aside to explain “the way of God more accurately”: how do you correct or help someone without humiliating them in public?
What did the disciples in Ephesus know and not know when Paul meets them, and what happens after he lays his hands on them?
What does the failure of the sons of Sceva show about using the “name” of Jesus, and what does it mean that the books of sorcery are burned in public?
The word ὁδός (hodos, “way”) appears as the name of the movement, “the Way”: what does this name suggest about how the first Christians understood their own faith?
What interests lie behind the riot stirred up by Demetrius, and how does the city clerk manage to calm the assembly?
Demetrius defends Artemis because the trade brings prosperity: at what point might money be influencing your convictions without your noticing?
What happens at the gathering in Troas on the first day of the week, and how does Paul react to Eutychus's fall?
In taking leave of the elders of Ephesus, how does Paul sum up his years of work with them, and why does he say he is “innocent of the blood of all men”?
Paul calls the elders ἐπίσκοπος (episkopos, “overseer”) and asks them to “shepherd” the church: what does this verse say about the nature of this task, and how do churches organize it today?
“It is more blessed to give than to receive”: in what relationship or concrete situation could you experience this sentence this week?
What does Agabus do with Paul's belt in Caesarea, how do the friends react, and what does Paul answer?

The disciples in Tyre say “through the Spirit” that Paul should not go up, and Paul says he goes bound by the Spirit: how should we understand these directions that seem to pull in different directions?
The word νόμος (nomos, “law”) appears in James's request and in the accusation in the temple: what rumor was going around about Paul and the Law, and how do the elders try to dispel it?
Paul accepts a rite of purification so as not to offend the Jewish brothers: in what situation would you give up a right to preserve living together?
How does Paul present himself to the crowd in Jerusalem, and in what language does he speak to obtain silence?
The word φῶς (phos, “light”) marks the account of the encounter on the road to Damascus: what does this light do to Saul, and how does he reach the city?
At what point in the speech does the crowd begin shouting again, and why does precisely that word provoke so much fury?
How does Paul's Roman citizenship change the way the authorities treat him, and why does he mention it only at this moment?
Ananias tells Paul he will be a witness “of what you have seen and heard”: of what have you been a witness in your own story with God?
How does the hearing before the Sanhedrin begin, and what strategy does Paul use when he realizes there are Pharisees and Sadducees?
Paul claims to have lived before God “in all good” συνείδησις (syneidesis, “conscience”): what does he mean by this, being someone who once persecuted the church?
What place does the Lord's word on the following night have in Paul's path to Rome, and what meaning does it give to the following chapters?
A young man, Paul's nephew, foils a plot of more than forty men: what small action of yours may carry more weight than it seems?
Of what does Tertullus accuse Paul before Felix, and how does he begin his speech?
The word αἵρεσις (hairesis, “sect, party”) is used by the accusers: how does Paul answer the label, and with what name does he himself describe the movement?
Felix hears Paul speak of righteousness, self-control and judgment and becomes afraid: why, even so, does he put it off and keep Paul in prison for two years?
“You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you”: what important decision have you been putting off, and what makes you wait?
What do the leaders in Jerusalem ask of Festus as soon as he takes office, and how does the hearing in Caesarea end with Paul's appeal?
The verb ἐπικαλέομαι (epikaleomai, “appeal”) is repeated to the end of the chapter: why does Paul use this right of a Roman citizen, and what door does it open?
How does Festus sum up the case for Agrippa, and what does the phrase “a dead man named Jesus, whom Paul claimed to be alive” reveal about a Roman's view of the matter?
Paul does not avoid answering, but neither does he accept being handed over unjustly: how do you balance humility and the defense of your rights?
How does Paul tell, before Agrippa, his own life before and after the road to Damascus, and what mission does he say he received?
The verb ἀπολογέομαι (apologeomai, “make a defense”) frames the speech: in what way does this defense go beyond a mere legal argument?
Festus calls Paul insane and Agrippa says “can you persuade me in such a short time?”: what does each reaction show about the one who makes it?
“I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision”: what call or conviction have you received that you are still learning to obey?
What warning does Paul give before leaving Fair Havens, why is he not heeded, and what happens after the northeaster arrives?
The verb εὐθυμέω (euthymeo, “take courage”) appears twice in Paul's speech on the ship: on what does he base this courage, in the middle of a storm with no sun and no stars?
What echoes might Paul's gestures have as he takes bread, gives thanks and breaks it before 276 people, most of them not Christians?
Everyone reaches land, “some on planks and some on pieces of the ship”: what “planks” helped you get through a hard stage?
How do the islanders of Malta treat the shipwrecked, and how does their opinion of Paul change after the episode of the viper?
Why does Acts end with Isaiah's words about hearing without understanding, and how can we read these words without turning them into a rejection of the Jewish people?
The book ends with the adverb ἀκωλύτως (akolytos, “unhindered”): what is the effect of closing the story with Paul in prison but the word free?
Acts ends without telling Paul's end, like an open story: what part of this story continues with you?
